title: Is Good Practice Too Babyish for Big Kids? Or Is That Just a Teacher Misconception?
author: Think Forward Educators
summary: This article confronts a persistent barrier to evidence-informed practice in secondary schools: the belief, held by many secondary teachers, that explicit instruction, scaffolding, and structured routine are appropriate for younger students but too 'babyish' or patronizing for older ones. The author, writing from a Year 5-12 school in regional Victoria, argues that this is a misconception rooted in confusing sophistication of content with sophistication of pedagogy. The cognitive architecture of learning does not change at Year 9: working memory remains limited, prior knowledge still determines what can be understood, and attention is still the gateway to learning. The article examines why evidence-informed practices that teachers can articulate in professional learning sessions do not consistently appear in secondary classrooms, identifying several root causes including subject-specific identity, assessment pressure, and the felt sense that 'telling' students things is somehow a failure of teaching. The piece is most valuable for school leaders and instructional coaches working to build consistent evidence-based practice across secondary schools, where the pedagogical identity of specialist subject teachers creates particular resistance.
points: The central misconception under examination is that explicit instruction and structured scaffolding are appropriate for primary students but condescending for secondary students — an assumption that confuses content complexity with pedagogical sophistication.

The cognitive science rebuttal is straightforward: working memory limits, the role of prior knowledge, and attention requirements do not change at secondary; the techniques that work for learning work at every age and every level of content.

Secondary teacher identity — the 'I am a historian who teaches' rather than 'I am a teacher who teaches history' orientation — is a real barrier to pedagogical consistency, because subject expertise can crowd out pedagogical knowledge.

Assessment pressure in secondary creates a paradox: the higher the stakes of learning, the more teachers revert to content coverage over structured practice — precisely when the evidence-based approaches would matter most.

The article's most useful implication for school leaders is that professional learning in secondary schools must address identity and belief (not just technique), because the resistance to good pedagogy is often a professional-identity protection, not ignorance.
quotes: If you’re reading this blog, you’re probably already familiar with the evidence underpinning cognitive load theory, explicit instruction, knowledge-rich curriculum and behaviour routines. There is little need to revisit the importance of applying cognitive load theory to lesson design, the enduring value of Rosenshine’s Principles of Instruction, or why building knowledge enables students to learn more.

At our Year 5–12 coeducational school in regional Victoria, we have spent countless hours leading professional learning around evidence-informed practice. Staff have explored cognitive load theory, interactive explicit instruction within a gradual release model, checks for understanding, formative assessment, responsive teaching and the importance of consistent school-wide routines.
Many explain that these strategies have simply become part of what school looks like. They have experienced them for years, understand their purpose and appreciate the clarity they provide.
This level of instructional expertise demands deep subject knowledge. By comparison, setting an open-ended research task can appear considerably easier.

Retrieval practice activates prior knowledge in long-term memory, reducing cognitive load as students encounter increasingly complex ideas. Successive questioning allows teachers to continually monitor understanding while strengthening memory.

These are simply observations gathered through informal conversations with staff and students in one school. However, discussions with colleagues across other schools suggest that these barriers are far from unique.

It is helping teachers feel confident enough to apply them consistently. If we can move beyond the perception that good teaching looks fundamentally different simply because students are older, we may discover that what secondary students need is not less structure, but better structure.
